newsitem.title: USA: Sundance festival honors films on young and middle aged.
newsitem.headline: Sundance festival honors films on young and middle aged.

text.p: The dramatic film "Sunday" and the documentary "Girls Like Us" captured the Grand Jury awards of the 13th Annual Sundance Film Festival Saturday night.
The awards were the culmination of the 10-day festival that is considered a premier showcase for independent films. The festival closes Sunday nigt.
More than 10,000 visitors slogged through snow-lined streets at this ski resort town sampling the more than 127 feature films and 56 short films.
"Sunday," directed by Jonathon Nossiter, portrayed a Sunday in the lives of a middle aged man and woman who have reached a dead end in their lives.

Their chance meeting gives them one last opportunity for love and redemption. "Sunday" also won the Waldo Salt screenwriting award, which was bestowed last year upon "Big Night," a modestly budget film that received critical and box office success.

"Girls Like Us," directed by Jane C. Wagner and Tina DiFeliciantonio, is a portrait of four teenaged girls from a working class neighbourhood in South Philadelphia. The coming-of-age film takes a four-year look at the girls, tracing their evolution toward sexuality.
The film "Hurricane", written and directed by Morgan J. Freeman, won the Audience Award in the dramatic category.
The dramatic Directing Award and the Cinematography Award also went to "Hurricane," a story of a club of boys who ride their bikes in lower Manahattan, stealing and getting into trouble with the law.
"Paul Monette: The Brink of Summer's End," a tribute to the late writer and AIDS activist, won the Audience Award in the documentary category. It was written and directed by Monte Bramer.

"Licensed to Kill," an examination of violence against gay men that focused on convicted murderers and their attitudes toward gays, was awarded the Film Makers' Trophy Award and the documentary Directing Award. It was written by Arthur Dong.

The Latin American Cinema Award was presented to "Landscapes of Memory," a story about two peasants whose paths cross in a background of crushing poverty and insatiable greed. The film, written and directed by Jose Araujo, was produced in Bazil.

The festival, originally called the U.S. Film Fetival, was taken over by actor-director Robert Redford and his Sundance Institute. While Redford opened the festival, he was not seen throughout the event because he was working on a movie, festival officials said.
